It holds only the three sample questions from the task spec.

questions.question: What is the growth outlook for South Asia in this report?
questions.reference_answer: Growth in South Asia is expected to soften to 6.3 percent in 2026, mainly because of the conflict in the Middle East (higher energy prices, reduced oil and gas supplies, disruptions to remittances and tourism); the forecast was marginally upgraded since January on stronger domestic demand and exports. Growth is set to pick up to an average of about 7 percent a year in 2027-28. India is projected to grow 6.6 percent in fiscal year 2026/27. (Figures must come from South Asia, not another region.)

questions.question: What does Chapter 3 say about sovereign debt in developing economies?
questions.reference_answer: Chapter 3 says rising government debt is a key challenge for EMDEs: it raises interest rates, debt-service costs and the likelihood of debt distress. EMDE government debt rose from under 40 percent of GDP in 2010 to over 70 percent. Higher debt is associated with higher dollar-denominated sovereign spreads and domestic-currency yields, non-linearly (bigger increases at higher debt levels); the rise since 2010 is associated with roughly 110 and 30 basis points higher spreads and yields. Effects are larger for countries with a history of default, low credit ratings, frontier status, short-term debt reliance or weak governance. It recommends strengthening fiscal positions (revenue mobilization, more efficient spending, better debt management, domestic debt markets, debt-for-development swaps). Any of these key points counts; it must not mix in other chapters' findings.

questions.question: According to the executive summary, what are the main risks to the global outlook?
questions.reference_answer: The executive summary says risks are skewed to the downside: a renewed escalation of hostilities or prolonged disruptions to commodity flows could raise commodity prices, intensify inflation and food insecurity, trigger financial stress and lower growth; if energy supply disruptions are more severe and come with substantial financial stress, global growth could fall to just 1.3 percent in 2026; persistent trade policy uncertainty, geopolitical strains and weather-related shocks are also material risks. On the upside, broader AI investment and adoption could lift activity.
